parole.testo: Attested since the 16th century. From Borrowed from Middle Low German brūken, from Old Saxon brūkan, from Proto-West Germanic *brūkan, from Proto-Germanic *brūkaną, cognate with Latin fruor (“enjoy”).
Borrowed from Middle Low German busse, from Old Saxon *buhsa, from Proto-West Germanic *buhsā. Cognate with Swedish bössa, Danish bøsse.
Borrowed from Middle Low German vrisch, from Old Saxon *frisk, *fersk, from Proto-West Germanic *frisk, from Proto-Germanic *friskaz. Doublet of ferskur.
Borrowed from Middle Low German gābe, from Old Saxon *gāva, from Proto-West Germanic *gābā (“gift, giving”).
From Middle Low German last, from Old Saxon *hlast, from Proto-West Germanic *hlasti (“burden, load”).

Borrowed from Middle Low German lucke, gelucke of uncertain ultimate origin, but perhaps related to Proto-West Germanic *lok (“shutter, lock”). Cognate with Faroese lukka, Norwegian Nynorsk lukke, Danish lykke, dialectal Swedish lycka. More at luck.

From Middle Low German proten (“to object, to grumble, to scold”), from Old Saxon *pratt, from Proto-West Germanic *prattu, probably ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *prattuz (“boastful talk”). Cf. Norwegian Bokmål prute, Norwegian Nynorsk prute, Swedish pruta.

Earliest attested in 18th century, from earlier pekill, attested a century earlier, presumably borrowed from Middle Low German pēkel, probably related to pecken (“to prick, sting”), from Old Saxon *pikkōn, from Proto-West Germanic *pikkōn.
Borrowed from Middle Low German röcklīn, diminutive of rock, from Proto-West Germanic *hrokk, from Proto-Germanic *hrukkaz (“robe, jacket”); compare German Röcklein.
Borrowed from Middle Low German spil, from Old Saxon spil, from Proto-West Germanic *spil (“game, dance”).

Likely borrowed from Middle Low German sterke (“starch, stiffness, strength”), from Old Saxon *sterkī, from Proto-West Germanic *starkī. Cognate with English starch, German Stärke (“starch”), dialectal Dutch sterk (“starch”). Compare also Swedish stärkelse (“starch”).

Borrowed from Middle Low German straffen, from Proto-West Germanic *strēpōn, of uncertain ultimate origin, but possibly related to *streupan (“to squeeze, press, graze”). Cognate with Swedish straff; compare with German Strafe.

parole.significato: to last, to continue, to go on
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle Low German waren (whence also Swedish vara, Norwegian vare, Danish vare), from Proto-West Germanic *waʀōn.
